title: The Yellow House
subtitle: Hope, Crisis and the Work of Recovery
introduction: In Arles, Vincent hoped to build a place where artists could live and work together. Gauguin’s arrival brought that possibility into the rooms of the Yellow House.

Their weeks together brought shared subjects, experiments with observation and memory, and uncertainty about the household’s future. On 23 December 1888, Vincent experienced a severe crisis and injured himself.
Follow the story through their correspondence, the reports of others, and the work Vincent made as he tried to resume his life.
contentNote: This story discusses self-injury and mental distress. No graphic imagery is shown.

entry.title: A Room for Gauguin
entry.paragraph: Vincent prepared the Yellow House for a life shared with another painter. Two sunflower paintings hung in the room intended for Paul Gauguin. The invitation carried his hope that artists could live and work together in the south.

chapters.label: A Place for Two
chapters.title: Gauguin Arrives
paragraphs: Gauguin arrived in Arles on 23 October 1888. Vincent had prepared the Yellow House and its sunflower paintings for a companion with whom he could live and work.
The invitation belonged to a larger hope: a community of artists in the south. In the next chapter, enter the daily arrangements and artistic experiments that made this first partnership real.

chapters.label: Working Side by Side
chapters.title: Two Artists in One House
paragraphs: Two painters now shared the Yellow House. Their partnership involved the work of keeping a home, making pictures and talking through what art could become.
Follow four parts of that shared life: a household becoming a studio, experiments with memory, a portrait of a companion, and the town beyond their door.

readings.label: A Shared Working Life
readings.title: A Household Becoming a Studio
paragraphs: Theo was part of this household even from Paris. His financial support and his work as an art dealer helped sustain Vincent and his arrangement with Gauguin. Vincent’s letters connect the sale and sending of paintings with the costs of living and working.

In early November, Vincent listed a chest of drawers, household utensils and twenty metres of canvas bought by Gauguin. They recorded the expenses for later repayment. Gauguin also had plans of his own, including another journey to Martinique.

Their working days took them to the Alyscamps, an avenue of tombs and tall poplars. Both made paintings there. Compare how the path recedes, how trees divide the surface, and how small the figures become. Neither canvas is simply a copy of what the eye sees.

people.name: Vincent
people.role: A home and a studio community
people.text: Invited Gauguin, prepared the rooms and hoped shared work could develop into a community of artists.

people.name: Paul Gauguin
people.role: A partner with plans of his own
people.text: Worked with Vincent, contributed household purchases and continued to consider his own artistic and travel plans.

people.name: Theo
people.text: Supported Vincent, sold work by Gauguin and remained involved through money, paintings and letters.

readings.label: Observation, Memory and Imagination
readings.title: How Does Experience Become a Painting?
paragraphs: Before Gauguin arrived, Vincent explained to Émile Bernard that an actual model or subject gave his work direction. Starting from life did not mean reproducing appearances mechanically: he could change colour, simplify forms and intensify expression.

Gauguin encouraged him to compose through memory and imagination. This was not a contest between a realist and an inventor. Both selected and transformed experience, and Vincent tried another way of bringing it into a picture.

Painted in Arles, Memory of the Garden at Etten brings an earlier place into a new scene. In a letter to Willemien, Vincent connected its figures and colours with their mother and Wil without claiming literal likenesses. Choose a detail below to follow his explanation.

observations.label: People
observations.text: The two foreground women can call their mother and Wil to mind without being their exact portraits. Vincent asks his sister to read associations in the figures rather than identify a literal family scene.

observations.label: Colour
observations.text: Dark violet clothing, an orange-and-green scarf and the emphatic garden colours help carry character and feeling. In his explanation, colour does more than describe the local appearance of things.

observations.label: Memory
observations.text: The painting was made in Arles, not in the Etten garden before his eyes. Earlier experience is reorganised in a new composition. Vincent links this experiment to conversations with Gauguin.

readings.label: Painting One Another
readings.title: Gauguin’s Image of Vincent
paragraphs: Gauguin painted Vincent seated at work on sunflowers, joining his companion to a subject already associated with him.

Museum research places the portrait in December, when Vincent was not painting fresh sunflowers. Memory and reference to earlier paintings shape this scene: it is Gauguin’s image of Vincent at work, not a transparent record of a sitting.

Look at the concentrated figure, the flowers and the act of painting. Gauguin’s later account of Vincent’s reaction is discussed in Sources & Versions, rather than staged here as a witnessed conversation.

readings.label: The Town After Dark
readings.title: Cafés, Brothels and Possible Subjects
readings.date: 1 or 2 November 1888 · An earlier café painting from September
paragraphs: Their shared life extended beyond the studio. In the joint letter to Émile Bernard of 1 or 2 November, Vincent reported going to brothels with Gauguin and discussed what might be painted there.
The letter supports a shared activity and a search for subjects. It does not establish how often either man went, every purpose or encounter, or a causal link with the later crisis.

The Night Café was painted in September 1888, before Gauguin’s arrival. It offers an earlier view of a café in Arles, not a brothel interior and not evidence of the two painters making this picture together.

chapters.label: Staying or Leaving
chapters.title: Sharing a House, Finding a Way
chapters.subtitle: Vincent and Gauguin in Arles
paragraphs: For Vincent, sharing the Yellow House meant more than having another painter nearby. It offered companionship, a household he could help sustain, and the possibility of a lasting studio in the south.

Gauguin brought his own ambitions and ways of working. Vincent admired him, tried unfamiliar approaches, and sometimes found that their discussions unsettled his confidence as well as extending his possibilities.

Follow the hopes and disagreements of these weeks before looking at the question of departure. Their relationship was not simply a friendship turning into hostility, nor a countdown to the crisis that followed.

sections.title: A Companion He Had Waited For
paragraphs: Vincent had spent months anticipating Gauguin’s arrival. In his letters, the prospect of working with someone he admired is bound up with the wish to feel less alone and to make a more sustainable life as a painter.

Sharing expenses could also ease the demands on Theo. Vincent wanted his work and the household to justify that support. Yet the two men did not necessarily imagine the same future: Vincent hoped to establish a studio in Arles, while Gauguin continued to think about returning to Martinique.

sections.title: What Should a Painting Begin With?
paragraphs: Vincent returned repeatedly to people, objects and places he could observe. He did not merely copy what he saw: colour, rhythm and simplification allowed him to convey what a subject meant to him.

Gauguin encouraged work from memory and imagination, reshaping a remembered scene rather than relying on a subject directly in front of him. Their differences concerned how an image could be made and felt, not a simple division between reality and fantasy.

sections.title: Trying His Friend’s Approach
paragraphs: Vincent was willing to experiment. In Memory of the Garden at Etten, he brought together remembered figures and a garden, following the invitation to work beyond immediate observation.

The experiment did not resolve his doubts. His letters describe learning from Gauguin but also feeling less at home with these imagined arrangements. Returning to portraits of the Roulin family offered another way forward. The earlier chapter’s painting study lets you examine that experiment without repeating it here.

sections.title: Disagreement at Close Quarters
paragraphs: Their discussions ranged from the painters they admired to models, technique and the treatment of paint. Living together meant that differences at the easel continued into the rooms they shared.

Vincent could praise Gauguin’s judgement while questioning whether a method suited his own work. The letters preserve admiration and unease together. They do not justify inventing a scene of humiliation, or diagnosing the relationship from a single disagreement.

sections.title: The Wish to Leave
paragraphs: By December, the household’s future was being discussed in correspondence with Theo. Reading the two men separately makes the difficulty more concrete: Vincent wanted the arrangement to continue, while Gauguin described the strain of sharing a home.

voices.title: Vincent to Theo
paragraphs: Vincent thought Gauguin was discouraged by Arles, the Yellow House and Vincent himself. He recognised that his friend might leave and said he would not insist on keeping him. He still hoped Gauguin might reconsider.

voices.title: Gauguin to Theo
paragraphs: Gauguin described incompatible temperaments and the difficulty of finding tranquillity while living together. He intended to return to Paris, yet also expressed respect for Vincent’s intelligence and regret about leaving.

sections.title: The Future of This Home
paragraphs: The decision was not fixed. In his letter of 17 or 18 December, Vincent described their visit to Montpellier and intense discussions of Delacroix and Rembrandt. The editors identify an accompanying letter in which Gauguin withdrew his earlier plan to return to Paris.

On 22 December, Gauguin told Émile Schuffenecker that he was staying for now, although leaving remained possible. This is Gauguin’s correspondence, cited in note 28 to Letter 726, not a decision voiced by Vincent. Their uncertain future was part of the setting for the crisis; it does not, by itself, explain why Vincent injured himself.

chapters.worksIntroduction: Vincent painted two chairs with different objects and atmospheres, giving the absent sitters distinct places in the house. Read them as an exploration of two personalities, not as a prediction of abandonment. Open either painting to look closer, then return to this story.

readings.label: Letters & Research
readings.title: Reading the December Correspondence
readings.date: Letters 724 and 726 · Dates established by the scholarly edition
paragraphs: The scholarly edition dates Letter 724 to on or about 11 December 1888. Earlier editions placed it on 23 December. Using the revised date matters: the possibility of Gauguin leaving was being discussed before the night of the crisis.

The annotations bring together Vincent’s letters and Gauguin’s correspondence with Theo and Schuffenecker. They are separate documents and perspectives, not a transcript of a conversation in the Yellow House.

chapters.label: 23 December
chapters.title: A Crisis in Arles
chapters.subtitle: The Evening and Its Aftermath
chapters.contentNote: This chapter discusses self-injury and a medical crisis. No graphic imagery is shown. You can continue directly to Care and Concern.
paragraphs: On 23 December 1888, Vincent suffered a severe crisis and injured his left ear. The Van Gogh Museum presents the injury as self-inflicted. Follow the events surrounding that night, then explore the explanations later proposed for it.
The records were made at different times and by people with different access to events. Keep the household’s tensions, the accounts of an encounter, and the question of Vincent’s motive distinct.

sections.title: Before the Night
sections.subtitle: A Shared Future in Question
paragraphs: By December, Gauguin had considered returning to Paris. Vincent recognised that their household might end, although their work and conversations continued and the decision to leave was reconsidered.
The previous chapter follows those changes in detail. They establish the pressures surrounding the household, but not the immediate cause of Vincent’s injury.

sections.title: Gauguin’s Account
sections.subtitle: An Encounter Remembered in Different Ways
paragraphs: Gauguin’s version reaches us through an early second-hand report and a memoir written much later. Compare what each account says, rather than turning either into an unqualified reconstruction of the night.

voices.title: Bernard’s Report to Albert Aurier
voices.badge: 1 JANUARY 1889 · BERNARD RETELLS WHAT GAUGUIN TOLD HIM
paragraphs: After Gauguin returned to Paris, Émile Bernard wrote that Vincent had followed him at night. Gauguin felt uneasy, spent the night in a hotel, and returned to find a crowd and police at the Yellow House.
This account does not mention Vincent approaching Gauguin with a razor. Bernard was not present in Arles that evening; he was recording what Gauguin had told him.

voices.title: Gauguin’s Later Recollection
paragraphs: Gauguin later described hearing familiar footsteps, turning and seeing Vincent approaching with an open razor. In this version, Vincent stopped and returned towards the house; Gauguin slept in a hotel.

Written about fifteen years after the event, this is Gauguin’s recollection, not an independently witnessed scene. The difference from Bernard’s earlier report is part of the evidence, not something to hide in a footnote.

sections.title: The Report from Arles
sections.subtitle: A Woman Called Rachel
paragraphs: The local newspaper reported that, on the preceding Sunday at about 11:30 p.m., Vincent went to a brothel, asked for a woman called Rachel and handed her his ear. The hour is a reported time, not a separately established timestamp.

According to the report, police went to his home the following morning, found him in bed in a grave condition and had him taken urgently to hospital. Later research into the woman’s identity belongs to the next chapter.

link.label: Meet the Woman Behind the Report →

sections.title: Asking Vincent Why
sections.subtitle: The Question Reached His Hospital Room
paragraphs: On 30 December, Dr Félix Rey told Theo that he had asked Vincent what had prompted him to cut his ear. Rey reported Vincent’s answer: “a purely personal matter”. The doctor had asked the question, but the reply does not let us reconstruct a motive.

The Saint-Rémy admission record of 8 May 1889 describes Vincent as retaining only a vague memory of the attack. This later medical observation and Rey’s contemporary letter are different records; neither supplies a complete account from Vincent of that night.

His letter of 2 January 1889 does preserve a wish for contact: he asked Theo to have Gauguin write to him. Beyond the search for a cause, there was a person seeking reassurance, care and a way back to everyday life.

readings.label: Why Did It Happen?
readings.title: Pressure, Health and Later Explanations
readings.date: Different kinds of evidence · Different degrees of certainty
readings.badge: EXPLANATIONS ARE NOT EQUIVALENT TO ESTABLISHED CAUSES
paragraphs: No surviving record gives a complete explanation from Vincent of why he injured himself that night. Later researchers have proposed answers, but an institutional account, a retrospective medical study and a disputed reconstruction do not carry the same evidential weight.

sections.title: Health and Household Pressure
paragraphs: The Van Gogh Museum places the injury within a severe mental crisis and the deteriorating relationship with Gauguin. This establishes a context, not a single recoverable motive.

A 2020 study by Willem Nolen and colleagues revisits the historical evidence and proposes interacting vulnerabilities involving mood, alcohol use, poor nutrition and mounting psychosocial pressures. It is a retrospective analysis, not a clinical examination of Vincent, and its diagnoses remain proposals.

The study’s discussion of probable alcohol-withdrawal delirium concerns episodes after the injury, during hospitalisation. It should not be retold as proof that alcohol withdrawal caused him to cut his ear.

sections.title: News from Theo
sections.badge: MARTIN BAILEY’S PROPOSED TRIGGER · NOT CONFIRMED
paragraphs: Martin Bailey proposes that news of Theo’s intended marriage to Jo may have arrived shortly before the crisis. Given Vincent’s reliance on his brother for companionship and financial help, Bailey considers whether the news could have added to his distress.

The letter Vincent received on 23 December has not survived. Its contents cannot be checked, and the scholarly editors do not establish when Theo first told him about the engagement. The proposed timing and trigger are Bailey’s interpretation, not a demonstrated cause of the crisis.

sections.title: An Alternative Injury Hypothesis
sections.badge: HANS KAUFMANN AND RITA WILDEGANS · DISPUTED RECONSTRUCTION
paragraphs: In their 2008 book, Kaufmann and Wildegans proposed that Gauguin injured Vincent with a sabre during a confrontation and that the artists concealed what had happened. Their argument draws inferences from discrepancies in the accounts and other circumstances.

It does not supply an established eyewitness account of a sword injury. The Van Gogh Museum continues to describe self-injury. This alternative belongs among attributed, contested interpretations, not under a promise to reveal what really happened.

sections.title: Why This Injury, and Why This Recipient?
sections.badge: TWO QUESTIONS · NO VERIFIED STATEMENT OF INTENTION
paragraphs: Explaining the injury is not the same as explaining why Vincent took the ear to this particular woman. Research into her life does not, by itself, reveal what he intended.
The next chapter separates her identity and history from unverified claims about healing a scar. It also follows the later visit Vincent described in his own letter.

link.label: Explore the Question of the Recipient →

readings.label: The Extent of the Injury
readings.title: A Doctor’s Retrospective Note
readings.date: Félix Rey to Irving Stone · 18 August 1930
readings.badge: HOLDING INSTITUTION · A DOCUMENT MADE FOUR DECADES LATER
paragraphs: Was only the earlobe injured, or the external ear? The scholarly edition discusses a note and sketches that Félix Rey, the doctor who treated Vincent, made for the writer Irving Stone on 18 August 1930. The document is held by the Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley.

The editors use this material to support removal of the external ear, rather than only its lobe. It is a treating doctor’s later recollection, not a hospital chart drawn in December 1888. No graphic illustration is displayed here; the linked institution page includes the injury drawing.

chapters.label: A Woman Called Rachel
chapters.title: The Woman Behind the Report
chapters.date: 23 December 1888 · A later visit on 2 February 1889
paragraphs: The newspaper calls her Rachel, without giving a surname or a biography. Behind that reported name was a person whose life has often disappeared from the story.

Bernadette Murphy’s later research identifies her as Gabrielle Berlatier, a farmer’s daughter who had survived a dog bite and treatment earlier that year. Martin Bailey subsequently published her surname. Murphy describes her as a maid, rather than a sex worker. These are attributed research findings, not facts established by the newspaper alone.

The previous chapter follows the night itself. Here, explore her name, her circumstances and Vincent’s account of a later visit. None establishes a romantic relationship or a certain reason for choosing her.
chapters.readingsLabel: THE NAME · THE PERSON · THE OPEN QUESTION

readings.label: The Report
readings.title: A Name in the Newspaper
paragraphs: The local newspaper’s item supplies the name Rachel, but no surname, age or account of her earlier life. It cannot, by itself, establish the later identification as Gabrielle Berlatier.

The scholarly letter edition reproduces the report and compares it with other accounts. The preceding chapter narrates its chronology; this panel focuses on what it tells us about the recipient, and what it leaves out.

The Van Gogh Museum’s account likewise describes self-injury and a visit to a brothel; it calls the recipient a prostitute. Murphy’s later research offers a different account of her occupation. An institutional summary, a contemporary report and later research should not be mistaken for the same kind of evidence.

readings.label: Tracing Gabrielle
readings.title: A Life Before That Night
readings.date: Medical history in 1888 · Research published in 2016
paragraphs: Murphy traced a young woman named Gabrielle but withheld her surname. Following clues in her book and medical records at the Institut Pasteur, Bailey identified her as Gabrielle Berlatier, a farmer’s daughter living near Arles.

Bailey reports that a rabid dog bit her left arm on 8 January 1888. Local cauterisation came before anti-rabies treatment in Paris. She was eighteen at treatment and nineteen by December. The injury left a scar; the journey and associated expenses placed pressure on her family.

Murphy describes work as a maid and cleaner at the brothel. The registration age for sex workers was twenty-one, but Bailey cautions that the rule was not always observed. Age alone therefore cannot settle her occupation.

Murphy also suggests she may have worked at the Café de la Gare, where Vincent lodged. That possible connection does not prove they already knew each other. The underlying medical documents are discussed through these researchers’ accounts; no reconstructed archive page is presented here.

readings.label: Why Her?
readings.badge: OPEN QUESTION · NO VERIFIED STATEMENT OF INTENTION
readings.title: A Scar Does Not Establish a Motive
readings.date: Identity research and the limits of a proposed explanation
paragraphs: Reports of Gabrielle’s earlier dog bite and treatment do not prove that Vincent knew about her scar, or that his injury was intended to repair it.

The specific claim that he imagined using his healthy flesh to heal her has not been verified here against a page-specific passage in Murphy’s original book. It should not be presented as a confirmed research finding or confidently attributed to her on the basis of secondary retellings.

Letter 745 describes a later visit and concern about her suffering. It does not state his intention on 23 December. The question remains open: neither a romantic gesture nor an act of rescue is established by these records.

readings.label: A Later Visit
readings.title: Returning to See Her
readings.date: Letter 745 · 3 February 1889 · Describing a visit on 2 February
paragraphs: On 3 February, Vincent told Theo that he had gone back the previous day to see the woman he had approached during the crisis. He wrote that she had suffered, had fainted and had since regained her composure. He also described her sympathetically, as someone of whom people spoke well.

The letter is a first-person record of a later visit, not a full account of the December night. It does not give her name or explain why he brought her the ear. It brings her distress back into view without confirming Murphy’s later identification or proposed motive.

chapters.label: Care and Concern
chapters.title: News from the Hospital
paragraphs: Gauguin sent a telegram to Theo on 24 December. Theo took the night train to Arles to see his brother in hospital. Gauguin left Arles in the days following the crisis.
Doctors and friends kept Theo informed. On 30 December, Félix Rey described an improvement in Vincent’s condition while acknowledging how difficult it was to answer Theo’s questions with certainty.
Rey also wrote about his own experience of being far from his family. His letter brings a personal voice into the record of Vincent’s care.

people.name: Theo van Gogh
people.text: Travelled to Arles and remained central to the correspondence about Vincent’s care.

people.name: Félix Rey
people.text: Reported improvement while acknowledging the limits of what he could know.

people.name: Joseph Roulin
people.text: Wrote to the family and accompanied Vincent after he left hospital.

readings.label: From the Doctor
readings.title: Félix Rey to Theo
paragraphs: Rey reports that Vincent’s condition has improved, but cannot offer certainty about what will follow. He also recalls his own separation from his family. Clinical observation and personal sympathy both have a place in this letter.

readings.label: From a Friend
readings.title: Joseph Roulin to Willemien
paragraphs: Roulin writes about Vincent’s return from hospital and his own efforts to accompany him. The letter presents recovery through the practical actions of a friend. Roulin accidentally wrote the year as 1888; the scholarly edition dates it to 1889.

chapters.label: Returning to Work
chapters.title: A Face in the Studio
paragraphs: Vincent returned home on 7 January. He told Theo that he intended to begin with still lifes to regain the habit of painting. He also planned a portrait of Félix Rey.
That month, he painted Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear. A canvas on an easel and a Japanese print appear behind him. The bandage records the injury within an image of himself as a working painter.

On 17 January, he reported that he had begun working again. The same letter counted hospital payments, laundry and other expenses. Recovery involved finding strength, paying bills and returning to his materials.

hotspots.label: The Bandage
hotspots.text: The injury was to Vincent’s left ear. Working from a mirror reversed his features: the bandage is on the figure’s right, which is the viewer’s left. This is a self-portrait in a studio, not an image of the injury itself.

hotspots.label: The Canvas
hotspots.text: A canvas on an easel stands behind him. Its presence brings the setting back to work: a room with the materials and possibilities of painting, not only a place of suffering.

hotspots.label: The Japanese Print
hotspots.text: The Japanese print on the wall recalls his sustained interest in Japanese art. Together with the easel, it places the injured man within the visual world of a working artist.

readings.label: 7 January · Returning Home
readings.title: Regaining the habit of painting
paragraphs: Home again, Vincent proposes starting with still lifes and making a portrait of Rey. These are plans for specific pieces of work, not evidence that his recovery is complete.

readings.label: 17 January · Work and Bills
readings.title: The practical life of recovery
paragraphs: Vincent reports returning to work while accounting for hospital costs, laundry and other expenses. Read these ordinary obligations beside the self-portrait: a life is being resumed through materials, money and care.

chapters.label: Living in Arles
chapters.title: Illness, Neighbours and Confinement
paragraphs: Further crises interrupted Vincent’s recovery. In February, a petition signed by thirty residents asked the authorities to have him committed.

The petition and police report recorded fears and allegations about his behaviour. Vincent’s letter of 19 March gives another view: he described being confined, distressed by the accusations and unable to use his studio.
Read together, these records reveal a difficult relationship between illness, public concern and personal freedom. Each document speaks from a particular position.

readings.label: The Petition
readings.title: A document of public concern
readings.date: February 1889 · Thirty signatures on the surviving petition
paragraphs: The petition records the residents’ fears and allegations. Their statements must remain attributed to the document, rather than being retold as established acts. The scholarly annotations link the petition and police material.

readings.label: Vincent’s Response
readings.title: Confinement and the inaccessible studio
paragraphs: Vincent describes confinement, distress over the accusations and his inability to use his studio. He says that more than eighty people signed, whereas the surviving petition bears thirty signatures. His experience and the surviving document should both be visible; neither number should silently replace the other.

chapters.label: Seeking a Place of Care
chapters.title: The Decision to Go to Saint-Rémy
paragraphs: In a letter to Willemien written between late April and early May, Vincent described repeated crises and his plan to enter an institution at Saint-Rémy.
He continued to think about the course of his work, the books he was reading and the life he hoped to regain.
On 8 May 1889, he entered Saint-Paul-de-Mausole. The admission documents record his wish for care and observation. His next year of painting would take shape within this new setting.

readings.label: Read About the Decision
readings.title: Seeking a setting for care and work
readings.date: Letter 764 · Between about 28 April and 2 May 1889
paragraphs: The letter to Willemien describes repeated crises and the proposed move. The admission register records his entry on 8 May. These are separate documents: the decision and the institutional record should not be presented as the same moment.

evidence.title: Gauguin’s Account
evidence.subtitle: A Recollection Written Later
paragraphs: In Avant et après, written in 1903, Gauguin described Vincent approaching him with an open razor. A letter from Émile Bernard to Albert Aurier dated 1 January 1889, reporting what Gauguin had told him, gives a different account of the encounter.
These texts reach us through different moments and narrators. They require comparison; neither is a recording of the evening.

evidence.title: The Extent of the Injury
evidence.subtitle: A Drawing by Félix Rey
paragraphs: Accounts differed over how much of the ear was removed. In 1930, Félix Rey drew the injury for the writer Irving Stone. Preserved at the Bancroft Library, the note and drawings support an injury involving almost the entire external ear.
The drawing was made decades after Rey treated Vincent. It is not an 1888 hospital chart.
evidence.contentNote: The external source includes a medical drawing of the injury. It is not displayed in this gallery.
evidence.linkLabel: View the Medical Drawing at Berkeley

evidence.title: The Woman in the Report
evidence.subtitle: Rachel and a Later Identification
paragraphs: The contemporary report uses Rachel. Murphy’s 2016 identification and Bailey’s subsequent archival work propose Gabrielle Berlatier and describe a young maid. Bailey also cautions against using the registration age alone to prove her occupation.
Letter 745 records a later visit but does not name her. Identity, occupation, acquaintance and motive are separate questions; establishing one would not automatically establish the others.

evidence.title: The Museum’s Account
evidence.subtitle: A present-day synthesis, not an eyewitness report
paragraphs: The Van Gogh Museum describes Vincent injuring himself on 23 December, wrapping the ear and taking it to a woman in a brothel. Its page calls her a prostitute. It does not establish a scar-healing motive.

This museum narrative supplies the exhibition’s basic sequence of crisis, care and renewed work. Its wording about the recipient should be compared with Murphy’s later occupation research, not silently combined with it.

evidence.title: An Explanation Is Not an Intention
evidence.subtitle: The limits of the scar-healing claim
paragraphs: Gabrielle’s documented treatment does not establish Vincent’s knowledge of a scar or an intention to heal it. The healthy-flesh explanation has not been verified against a specific passage in Murphy’s original book; secondary retellings are not sufficient to attribute it as a confirmed finding.

Letter 745 records concern and a later visit, not his intention on the night of the injury. This exhibition leaves that intention unresolved and does not turn self-injury into a romantic gesture or successful act of rescue.

evidence.title: An Alternative Reconstruction
evidence.subtitle: The Gauguin Hypothesis
paragraphs: In their 2008 book, Hans Kaufmann and Rita Wildegans proposed that Gauguin injured Vincent with a sabre and that the artists concealed what had happened.

This is a later reconstruction advanced by those authors. It differs from the Van Gogh Museum’s account of self-injury. The presence of several narratives does not give them the same evidential weight.

evidence.title: The Portrait and a Later Reaction
evidence.subtitle: Gauguin’s retrospective voice
evidence.badge: LATER RECOLLECTION · NOT A WITNESSED DIALOGUE
paragraphs: The museum catalogue discusses Gauguin’s later claim that Vincent recognised himself in the sunflower portrait but thought he looked like a madman. This reaction reaches us through Gauguin’s retrospective account, not a contemporary transcript of Vincent speaking.
Read it as evidence of how Gauguin later told the story. It should not be turned into invented speech or used to diagnose Vincent from the painting.

sources.title: Letter 712 · Vincent to Theo
sources.note: Describes Gauguin’s arrival on 23 October and the practical hopes of the household.

sources.title: Letter 716 · Vincent and Gauguin to Émile Bernard
sources.note: A shared document containing writing by both painters. The reader uses editorial summaries, not invented dialogue.

sources.title: Letter 724 · Vincent to Theo
sources.note: The current scholarly edition dates this letter to around 11 December; older editions placed it on 23 December.

sources.title: Letter 726 · Vincent to Theo
sources.note: Vincent’s account of artistic discussions; note 28 identifies Gauguin’s accompanying retraction of departure and his 22 December letter to Schuffenecker. These are separate voices and documents.

sources.title: Letter 728 · Vincent to Theo, with annotations
sources.note: Annotations include the newspaper report of 30 December and compare accounts of the crisis, including later recollections.

sources.title: Félix Rey to Theo · FR 1056
sources.note: Rey reports Vincent’s answer when asked about his motive, along with his condition and uncertainty about recovery. It is a doctor’s contemporary report of a reply, not a full explanation from Vincent.

sources.title: Joseph Roulin to Willemien · FR b710
sources.note: A friend’s account of accompanying Vincent after hospital. The mistaken year on the letter is discussed by the editors.

sources.title: Letter 732 · Vincent to Theo
sources.note: Return home, planned still lifes and the portrait of Félix Rey.

sources.title: Letter 736 · Vincent to Theo
sources.note: Painting again alongside hospital payments, laundry and other expenses.

sources.title: Letter 750 · Vincent to Theo
sources.note: Distinguishes allegations from Vincent’s account. Vincent mentions more than eighty signatures; the surviving petition has thirty.

sources.title: Letter 764 · Vincent to Willemien
sources.note: Repeated crises and the decision to enter an institution at Saint-Rémy.

sources.title: Saint-Paul-de-Mausole · Admission register
sources.note: Records admission, the wish for care and observation, and the vague memory of the earlier attack. It is a later institutional record, distinct from Rey’s December letter and Vincent’s decision to seek care.

sources.title: National Gallery · Sunflowers
sources.note: The sunflower paintings and the room prepared for Gauguin. The linked work is the London version, not a later repetition.

sources.title: The Courtauld · Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear
sources.note: The mirror reversal, easel, Japanese print and renewed commitment to painting. This is not the separate self-portrait with a pipe.

sources.title: Van Gogh Museum · Vincent’s Illness and the Healing Power of Art
sources.note: The museum’s account of self-injury, care and continuing work. The story does not infer a diagnosis or a single direct cause.

sources.title: UC Berkeley Library · The Tale of the Van Gogh Note
sources.note: Rey’s note for Irving Stone is held by the Bancroft Library. The external page includes an injury drawing; no graphic image is embedded here.

sources.title: Martin Bailey · Name of Mystery Woman Who Received Van Gogh’s Ear Revealed for First Time
sources.note: Reports Murphy’s account of Gabrielle as a maid at the brothel and Bailey’s archival identification of her surname as Berlatier. These are later research claims, separate from the 1888 report.

sources.title: Hans Kaufmann and Rita Wildegans · Authors’ Argument
sources.note: The proponents’ account of the sabre hypothesis, not a contemporary witness or the museum’s conclusion.

sources.title: Van Gogh Letters · Copyright and Permissions
sources.note: The reader links to the digital edition. Its manuscript images and extended translations have not been reprinted or treated as freely licensed.

sources.title: Le Forum Républicain · Chronique locale
sources.type: Contemporary newspaper report · Reproduced in the scholarly letter edition
sources.note: The annotations reproduce the local report about 23 December. Its name Rachel, chronology and reported words are distinguished from later identity research.

sources.title: Letter 745 · Vincent to Theo
sources.note: Vincent describes a visit the previous day, 2 February. The letter does not name the woman or state a scar-healing intention.

sources.title: Bernadette Murphy · Searching for ‘Rachel’
sources.type: Author’s published book excerpt · Identity research
sources.note: An excerpt concerning the identity research. It is not used here as verification of the specific healthy-flesh or scar-healing interpretation; that attribution requires a checked passage and page in the original book.

sources.title: Martin Bailey · Uncovering Van Gogh’s Infamous Days in Arles
sources.note: Bailey reviews Murphy’s identification and cautions that the age-twenty-one registration rule was not always observed. It is not decisive proof of occupation.

sources.title: Letter 665 · Vincent to Émile Bernard
sources.note: An artists’ studio in the south and the sunflower decoration planned before Gauguin’s arrival.

sources.title: Letter 698 · Vincent to Émile Bernard
sources.note: Actual models, changes of colour and simplification; this letter is to Bernard, not Theo, and is dated October, not September.

sources.title: Letter 717 · Vincent to Theo
sources.note: The Alyscamps paintings, Gauguin’s purchases, recorded expenses and his Martinique plans. Letter 717, rather than 715, supports this pairing.

sources.title: Letter 720 · Vincent to Willemien
sources.note: Vincent explains the people, expressive colours and remembered setting of Memory of the Garden at Etten.

sources.title: Kröller-Müller Museum · Falling Leaves (Les Alyscamps)
sources.note: Identifies the Vincent canvas used in the comparison: F486 / JH1620 / KM 108.668. Other Alyscamps versions are not substituted.

sources.title: Musée d’Orsay work · Gauguin’s Les Alyscamps
sources.type: Artwork and public-domain image record · Wikimedia Commons
sources.note: Identifies the Musée d’Orsay work RF 1985 68 and records the PD-Art status of its reproduction. This is the comparison image, not a Vincent painting.

sources.title: Van Gogh Museum Research Catalogue · Vincent van Gogh Painting Sunflowers
sources.note: Research on the portrait’s constructed scene, sunflower imagery and Gauguin’s later account of Vincent’s reaction. Reproduction rights are linked beneath the image.

sources.title: Yale University Art Gallery · The Night Café
sources.note: Identifies the September café painting, made before Gauguin’s arrival. It is not a brothel scene or a record of joint work.

sources.title: Letter 715 · Vincent to Theo
sources.note: Vincent on Gauguin’s arrival, companionship, health and the prospects of working together.

sources.title: Letter 721 · Vincent to Theo
sources.note: Working with Gauguin, artistic discussion and experiments with imagination; read alongside the earlier letter to Willemien.

sources.title: Letter 723 · Vincent to Theo
sources.note: Vincent’s doubts about the remembered garden, his Roulin portraits and his appreciation of Gauguin’s recent work.

sources.title: National Gallery · Van Gogh’s Chair
sources.note: The paired chairs as representations of two people and their different characters, not evidence of a predicted departure.

sources.title: Émile Bernard to Albert Aurier · The Early Retelling
sources.type: Contemporary second-hand letter · Quoted in the scholarly edition
sources.note: The annotations reproduce Bernard’s report of what Gauguin told him. Bernard was not an eyewitness in Arles; this early version does not mention a razor attack on Gauguin.

sources.title: The Courtauld · Gauguin’s Avant et après Manuscript
sources.type: Author’s later memoir · Holding institution’s manuscript project
sources.note: Gauguin’s account of Vincent approaching with a razor was written about fifteen years later. It is compared with Bernard’s earlier retelling, not staged as an independently verified scene.

sources.title: Willem Nolen and Colleagues · New Vision on the Mental Problems of Vincent van Gogh
sources.type: Peer-reviewed retrospective study · International Journal of Bipolar Disorders 8, 30
sources.note: DOI: 10.1186/s40345-020-00196-z. Assessment of historical evidence, not a clinical examination of Vincent. The proposed withdrawal deliriums follow the injury; they are not established as its cause.

sources.title: Martin Bailey · Was Van Gogh’s Mutilation of His Ear Connected to His Brother’s Engagement?
sources.type: Author’s research interpretation · Not a peer-reviewed medical study
sources.note: Bailey proposes the marriage news as an additional trigger, not the fundamental cause. The 23 December letter is lost, and the timing of the news is not established by the letter editors.

mediaNote: Painting reproductions follow the gallery’s credited public-domain records.
